title: Enforce the singleton property with a private constructor or an enum type
concept: A singleton is a class instantiated exactly once. Making the constructor private prevents normal client instantiation, but reflection attacks (via AccessibleObject.setAccessible) and deserialization can still create multiple instances unless specifically defended against with readResolve(). A single-element enum type is the most concise, bulletproof way to implement a singleton, providing free serialization safety and ironclad protection against reflective attacks.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: What is the best, most robust approach to implement a singleton in Java?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: A single-element enum type. It provides complete protection against reflection attacks, serializes without extra effort, and is concise.

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: When can you NOT use an enum type for a singleton?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: When your singleton must extend a superclass (other than Enum). In that scenario, use a private constructor with a static factory or field, defend against reflection in the constructor, and add readResolve() if serializable.

quiz.question: Why is a single-element enum considered the gold standard for implementing singletons in modern Java?
options: It provides ironclad protection against reflection attacks and guarantees safe serialization automatically
It runs faster by compiling directly into native assembly
Enums can extend any arbitrary superclass
Enums do not consume memory until accessed

quiz.question: What happens if a client attempts to use reflection (Constructor.newInstance) on an enum constructor?
options: It creates a second enum instance successfully
The JVM throws an IllegalArgumentException: 'Cannot reflectively create enum objects'

quiz.question: If a traditional class-based singleton implements Serializable, what must you do to prevent deserialization from creating a new instance?
options: Implement a readResolve() method that returns the existing INSTANCE

quiz.question: How can a traditional class-based singleton defend its private constructor against reflective invocation?
options: Throw an exception inside the constructor if it is invoked when the instance already exists

quiz.question: What is one limitation of using an enum as a singleton?
options: It cannot extend another superclass (it already implicitly extends java.lang.Enum)

interview_questions.question: Why does Joshua Bloch advocate for using an enum to implement singletons over the classic private constructor approach?
interview_questions.model_answer: Enums are inherently thread-safe, inherently serializable (preventing duplicate instances on deserialization), and the JVM strictly prohibits instantiating enums via reflection, providing complete safety with virtually zero boilerplate.

interview_questions.question: A developer implements a singleton by making the constructor private and implementing Serializable, but forgets `readResolve()`. What bug occurs?
interview_questions.model_answer: Every time an instance of the serialized class is deserialized, Java creates a brand new instance of the object regardless of constructor privacy, breaking the singleton guarantee.

interview_questions.question: What happens when you serialize an enum singleton versus a traditional object singleton?
interview_questions.model_answer: For enums, Java only serializes the enum constant's name. During deserialization, `Enum.valueOf()` is used to resolve the existing constant, guaranteeing identical identity without needing `readResolve()`. For standard objects, a new instance is allocated unless `readResolve()` overrides it.

interview_questions.question: How would you implement lazy-initialization for a singleton without synchronization overhead if you cannot use an enum?
interview_questions.model_answer: Use the Bill Pugh Initialization-on-demand holder idiom: define a private static inner class that holds the singleton instance. The inner class is not loaded into memory until `getInstance()` is called, giving thread-safe lazy initialization guaranteed by class loading semantics without explicit synchronization.
